titre: Duverger's Law (1951): How the Voting System Shapes the Number of Parties
accroche: Why do the British almost always vote for two parties when the French count half a dozen?
contenu_vulgarise:
In the United Kingdom as in the United States, national political life almost always comes down to a duel between two parties, despite the dozens of small groupings on the ballot. In France, by contrast, half a dozen parties regularly share the seats in the National Assembly. In 1951, in his book *Les partis politiques* (*Political Parties*), the French political scientist Maurice Duverger proposed an explanation that has to do neither with national temperament nor with each country's own history, but with the voting system itself.

## Tactical Voting: A Mechanism Rather Than a Choice

In single-member plurality voting in one round (a single round, a single seat per district, the candidate who finishes first wins), voting for a small party most often amounts to voting for nothing: if that party has no chance of finishing first in the district, the vote counts toward no seat. A voter who prefers that small party but fears above all the lead of the candidate they like least therefore has an interest in falling back on the big party best placed to beat that candidate. This reasoning, repeated district after district by millions of voters, mechanically pushes the political landscape toward two dominant blocs, without any law forbidding the creation of a third party, and without any voter needing to coordinate with the others.

## Two Other Voting Systems, Two Other Equilibria

Duverger contrasts this case with two other configurations. Proportional representation, which allocates seats in proportion to the votes obtained, removes most of the risk of voting for a minority party: a group that wins only 8% of the vote can still get members elected, which, on the contrary, encourages the multiplication of parties rather than their merger. Two-round majority voting, used in France for legislative elections, opens a third path: several close parties can run separately in the first round to gauge their respective strengths, then coordinate in the second round behind the best-placed one, which allows a multipartism organized in blocs, neither the forced merger of the British system nor the fragmentation of full proportional representation. The rule is by no means absolute, however: Canada and India, both with single-member plurality voting in one round, maintain several parties thanks to electoral bases concentrated region by region rather than dispersed across the nation, Duverger spoke of a tendency, not a theorem, and political scientists continue to discuss its limits as much as its scope.

repere.texte: In the United States, the two dominant parties have won on average 98% of all federal and state seats: one of the figures most often cited to illustrate Duverger's law.

carte.punch: United Kingdom: almost always two parties. France: half a dozen. Duverger points to the voting system.
carte.idee: In 1951, Maurice Duverger argued that one-round voting mechanically pushes toward two parties, through tactical voting, whereas proportional representation favors their multiplication. He spoke of a tendency: Canada and India, under the same voting system, keep several parties thanks to regional bases.

quiz.question: Why does single-member plurality voting in one round tend to produce only two dominant parties?
choix: Because the constitutions of many countries explicitly limit the number of authorized parties to two
Because voters under this system are by nature less politically divided
Because voting for a small party with no chance of winning amounts to voting for nothing, which pushes voters toward tactical voting
Because the parties themselves choose to merge by formal agreement before each election
quiz.explication: Nothing forbids a third party: it is the risk of having one's vote count toward no seat that pushes voters to fall back on the big party best placed to beat the one they like least, district after district.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What effect does Duverger attribute to proportional representation?
choix: It forces small parties to merge before each election
It brings the political landscape back toward two large, stable blocs
It prevents minority groups from winning a single member
It removes the risk of voting for a minority party and encourages the multiplication of parties
quiz_supplementaire.explication: With seats allocated in proportion to the votes, a group at 8% can get members elected: voting for a small party is no longer wasted, so parties multiply instead of merging.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why do Canada and India qualify Duverger's law?
choix: Their regional parties have concentrated electoral bases, which keeps them alive despite one-round voting
They apply full proportional representation in all their elections
Their constitutions require a minimum number of parties to be represented in Parliament
Their voters refuse on principle to vote tactically
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Voting there is single-member and one-round, but parties solidly rooted region by region win seats: Duverger spoke of a tendency, not a theorem.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does two-round majority voting allow, according to the entry?
choix: A forced merger into two parties, as in the United Kingdom
Total fragmentation, with every party remaining isolated to the end
A multipartism organized in blocs, with coordination in the second round
The elimination of any party that did not finish first everywhere
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Several close parties measure themselves in the first round, then coordinate in the second behind the best-placed one: neither the British merger nor the fragmentation of proportional representation.
